title: Lancaster at Wallace’s Crossroads
summary: Lancaster grew at Wallace’s Crossroads as the seat of Garrard County, carved in December 1796 as Kentucky’s 25th county and named for Gov. James Garrard.
bodyMarkdown:
[Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster,_Kentucky), the seat of Garrard County, grew from Maj. Andrew Wallace's settlement at a place called Wallace's Crossroads. It lies about 11 miles east of [Danville](/stories/danville-and-constitution-square/) and 3 miles east of the Dix River.

## Early settlers

Settlers reached the area before the town existed. A [state historical marker at the town spring](https://history.ky.gov/markers/lancaster-public-spring) records that in early 1776 John Wilson and Andrew Cowan built two small cabins nearby. In October 1782 James Speed settled near the spring.

## A new county and its seat

[Garrard County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Garrard_County,_Kentucky) was formed on December 6, 1796, from parts of Lincoln, Madison and Mercer counties. It was Kentucky's 25th county. It was [named for James Garrard](https://history.ky.gov/markers/garrard-county-1797), then governor. Garrard was a Virginia native and Revolutionary militia officer who came to Kentucky in 1783 and served in the statehood conventions at Danville.

Capt. William Buford donated the land for the county seat around Wallace's settlement. One account dates his gift to 1797; another gives 1798 as the year Lancaster was established. Buford chose the spring to supply water for the new court, and it served as Lancaster's public water source for nearly 50 years. Joseph Bledsoe Jr. surveyed and platted the town.

It was named for Lancaster, Pennsylvania, either because a settler came from there or because the plan was similar.

## Growth

A post office opened in 1801 under the name "Lancaster Court House," used until 1811. The town had 103 people in 1800 and 260 in 1810. The state assembly formally incorporated Lancaster in 1837. Buford's son Thomas became county sheriff in 1803 and later served in the legislature.

His house, the [Buford-Salter House](https://history.ky.gov/markers/buford-salter-house), was built around 1820 on lot 46 of the original plat.

## War and conflict

In August 1861 Union Gen. William "Bull" Nelson set up Camp Dick Robinson in Garrard County. It was the first federal military camp south of the Ohio River. Lancaster was briefly occupied by Confederate forces until they withdrew after the Battle of Perryville in 1862. In August 1874 a disputed county election, decided by 11 votes amid efforts to organize newly enfranchised Black voters, led to the Kennedy-Sellers Riot.

## Kentucky today

Lancaster remains Garrard County's seat. U.S. 27 runs through town toward Lexington, 35 miles north, and Somerset, 39 miles south. Its 2020 census population was 3,901. The town is also home to the Kennedy House, sometimes said to have been the setting for *Uncle Tom's Cabin*.
